section.title: Head Coverings in Worship
section.sectionRationale: Turning to the conduct of public worship, Paul commends the Corinthians for holding the traditions and then corrects their practice of head coverings. He grounds his instruction in an order of headship, God, Christ, man, and woman, and in the creation account, yet he balances it at once: in the Lord man and woman are interdependent, and everything comes from God. The passage teaches an abiding truth about honor, order, and the glad distinction of the sexes in worship, expressed in a first-century custom, and it calls the church to worship in a way that honors God and one another.
section.thesis: In public worship the order of headship, God over Christ, Christ over man, man over woman, is to be honored, so that men and women worship in ways that bring honor rather than shame; yet in the Lord man and woman are mutually dependent, for woman came from man and man is born of woman, and everything comes from God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the order of headship and the honor of covered or uncovered heads in worship; man as the image and glory of God, woman the glory of man, and the sign of authority; and the balancing truth that in the Lord man and woman are interdependent, everything coming from God.

verses.text: Now I commend you for remembering me in everything and for maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on to you.
But I want you to understand that the {{kephale|head}} of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.
Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head.
And every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is just as if her head were shaved.
If a woman does not cover her head, she should have her hair cut off. And if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or shaved off, she should cover her head.
A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the {{eikon|image}} and {{doxa|glory}} of God; but the woman is the glory of man.
For man did not come from woman, but woman from man.
Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
For this reason a woman ought to have a sign of {{exousia|authority}} on her head, because of the angels.
In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.
For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God.
Judge for yourselves: Is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered?
Doesn’t nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him,
but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering.
If anyone is inclined to dispute this, we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God.

kephale.gloss: Head. Used here in a relational sense within an ordered series, God, Christ, man, woman. Interpreters weigh whether it stresses authority or source, or both together, but the term sets a pattern of honor and order that the Trinity itself displays, since even Christ has God as His head without any lessening of His deity.

eikon.gloss: Image, a visible representation that reflects its original. Man is called the image and glory of God, echoing the creation of humanity in God's image, so that in worship he is to reflect God's honor. The word ties the passage back to Genesis and to the dignity of bearing God's likeness.

doxa.gloss: Glory, honor, that which displays the worth of another. Man is the glory of God and woman the glory of man, and a woman's long hair is her glory. The word runs through the passage as its key idea: worship is to render honor rightly, each reflecting glory in the place God has given.

exousia.gloss: Authority. The woman is to have a sign of authority on her head. Read as authority she is under, it marks her place in the ordered household of worship; read as her own authority to pray and prophesy, it dignifies her active part in the assembly. Either way it is a mark of her rightful standing in worship.

basic.context: Paul now takes up how the church behaves in public worship, beginning with head coverings for men and women. He commends the Corinthians for keeping the traditions he handed on, then teaches an order of relationships: the head of every man is Christ, the head of woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. In the culture of the day, a man praying with his head covered and a woman praying with her head uncovered each brought shame, so Paul urges them to worship in a way that honors this order. He roots it in creation, man made in God's image, woman made from and for man, yet he immediately balances it: in the Lord neither is independent of the other, and everything ultimately comes from God. Notably, women pray and prophesy in the assembly; the question is how, not whether.
basic.hermeneutics: This is one of the harder passages to apply, because it wraps an abiding principle inside a specific first-century custom. The enduring truths are the order of headship, the glad distinction of men and women, and worship that honors God and one another. Faithful Christians differ on whether the covering itself binds the church today or whether it was the cultural expression of a principle that now takes other forms. Paul himself invites the church to judge for yourselves and appeals to what honors God.
basic.originalLanguages: The key term is kephale, head, set in an ordered series from God to Christ to man to woman. Man is called the eikon, image, and doxa, glory, of God, echoing Genesis, while woman is the glory of man. A woman is to have a sign of exousia, authority, on her head, whether the authority she stands under or her own authority to take part. Through it all runs doxa, glory or honor, the passage's central concern.
basic.typology: The language of image and glory reaches back to Genesis, where humanity is made in God's image. Christ, the true image of God, restores that likeness, and the ordered relationships of worship reflect in a creaturely way the order within the Godhead, where the Son honors the Father as His head without any loss of equal deity.
basic.christ: Christ stands within the very order Paul describes: the head of Christ is God, yet the Son is fully divine, equal with the Father, and honors Him freely. This dismantles any idea that being under a head means being lesser in worth. As man is called to honor Christ his head and woman to honor rightly in worship, all of it is patterned on the Son who gladly honors the Father, and it points to Christ the true image of God in whom our dignity is restored.
basic.god: God is the source and goal of the whole order: the head of Christ is God, and everything comes from God. He is not a God of confusion but of honor and order, and He has made men and women different and interdependent for His glory. The passage guards both the dignity of God's image in humanity and the beauty of the distinctions He built into creation.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis tells of humanity made in God's image and of woman formed from man. Later in this letter Paul says God is not a God of disorder but of peace in the assemblies. Galatians declares that in Christ there is neither male nor female, all one in Him. Ephesians speaks of headship shaped by self-giving love.
basic.oneStory: From creation God made humanity in His image, male and female, distinct and made for one another. Sin twisted these relationships into domination and rivalry, but in Christ they are being restored to honor and mutual dependence, all things coming from God. This passage, for all its cultural distance, belongs to that story of a people learning again to worship in a way that reflects the honor and order of God Himself.

context.literary: Verses 2 to 16 are built like a sandwich. Praise opens the unit in verse 2 and an appeal to the universal practice of the churches closes it in verse 16, so the whole argument is wrapped in the language of tradition. Inside that frame Paul argues in rounds, and each round uses a different kind of reason. Verse 3 states an ordered series, with the word head repeated in each clause. Verses 4 to 6 turn on shame and run in strict parallel: every man who prays or prophesies with something on his head, every woman who does so uncovered. The parallel works because head carries two senses at once, the physical head that is covered or bare and the one it stands for, so that dishonoring one's head reaches further than the scalp. Verses 7 to 10 argue from Genesis and end on the puzzling words about the angels. Then verse 11 turns on a small hinge, in the Lord, however, and verses 11 and 12 set woman from man beside man through woman, reversing the order of verses 8 and 9 so that neither sex is left with a boast. The unit closes with three appeals that are not exegesis at all: judge for yourselves, nature itself, and the practice of the churches, verses 13 to 16. Paul uses scripture, shame, nature and custom together, which tells us he does not treat any single one as the whole case. The passage opens chapters 11 to 14 on the assembly, and it prepares for the Lord's Supper and the gifts, since all three concern what happens when the church comes together.
context.historical: Corinth was refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC, a trading city on the isthmus with a mixed population of freed people, merchants and settlers, proud of its new fortunes and eager for status. Paul founded the church there around AD 50 and wrote this letter from Ephesus about five years later, 1 Corinthians 16:8. In the Greco-Roman world what one wore on the head, and how one wore the hair, spoke about sex, rank and respectability. Roman men commonly drew a fold of the toga over the head when offering sacrifice, so a man praying with his head covered could look like a pagan priest at the altar. Respectable women were generally expected to cover their hair in public, and a woman with her hair loose or cropped could be taken to be shameless or to be breaking with her household. The exact first-century practice, what kind of covering, how common, and whether it was a veil or hair worn up, is debated, and Paul's own words in verses 6 and 15 leave room for more than one picture. We also need to hear the mood of the congregation. These were people who said everything is permissible, 1 Corinthians 6:12, and who thought they had already arrived, 1 Corinthians 4:8. A church caught up in the Spirit and in baptismal unity, Galatians 3:28, could easily conclude that distinctions between men and women no longer mattered in worship. Paul answers by praising what they kept and correcting what threatened to bring shame on them in the eyes of the Lord and of neighbors.
context.canonical: Paul builds on the first chapters of Genesis. Man as the image of God goes back to Genesis 1:26 and 27, and the order of woman from man in verses 8 and 9 recalls Genesis 2:18 to 23, where the woman is taken from the man and brought to him. He reads both chapters together, and verses 11 and 12 show that he does not use Genesis 2 to cancel Genesis 1, where male and female are made in the image alike. The same letter assumes that women pray and prophesy aloud in the assembly, which fits the Old Testament, where Miriam, Deborah and Huldah speak for God, Exodus 15:20, Judges 4:4 and 2 Kings 22:14. It fits Joel's promise that sons and daughters will prophesy, Joel 2:28 and 29, which Peter says Pentecost fulfilled, Acts 2:17 and 18, and it fits Philip's four prophesying daughters, Acts 21:9. It sits in tension with 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 35, and readers must hold the two passages together. The language of headship returns in Ephesians 5:23 to 25, where the head is also the one who gives himself up, and in 1 Corinthians 15:24 to 28, where the Son submits to the Father. The theme of the veil and glory reaches forward to 2 Corinthians 3:12 to 18, where believers with unveiled faces reflect the Lord's glory. Paul's creation arguments are found again in 1 Timothy 2:11 to 13, so this passage belongs to a pattern of apostolic teaching and is not a lonely oddity.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Paul wrote to people who were enthusiastic, newly free and in danger of confusing freedom with having no shape. He does not forbid women to pray and prophesy; he takes it for granted, and he gives the verbs to men and women alike in the same sentence. His concern is how they do so. He wants worship that does not dishonor the head, whether that means the woman herself, the man, or the Christ who stands over both, and he wants the church to be seen by its neighbors as honorable. The argument is a pastor's rather than a lawyer's: he reminds them of what he taught, gives several reasons, invites them to judge for themselves, and ends with the settled custom of the churches, not with a threat. Three aims run together. He wants the order he calls headship acknowledged without anyone being demeaned, he wants the God-given difference of men and women to be glad and visible and not erased, and he wants the pivot of verses 11 and 12 heard, so that no man imagines that he can boast over woman and no woman imagines that she can do without man. First hearers were meant to leave understanding that in the Lord dependence runs both ways and that everything finally comes from God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The passage mixes things that are commanded with things that are only reported. Paul commends the tradition, states an order of relationships, and gives reasons from creation. All of that is teaching. Where the passage points to hairstyles, the look of a bare head in Corinth, and the practice of other churches, it is speaking of the customs of its day, and it openly appeals to them. A useful way of applying such a passage is to ask what Paul argues from. He argues from the order of creation, from honor and shame, from what the surrounding culture reads in a gesture, and from the practice of the churches. The first of these does not change. The others show how the principle looked in Corinth. That is why faithful churches have landed in different places: some keep a covering, some hold that the covering was the local form of the principle, and some stress the hair as the covering Paul names in verse 15. It is wise to hold your own practice with the same humility Paul shows in verse 16, to refuse to turn the passage into a charter for silencing women, which it does not say, and equally to refuse to treat it as a mere piece of antique manners, which would ignore the creation reasons he gives.

debates.question: Does the covering bind the church today, or was it the local form of a lasting principle?

views.label: A lasting symbol
views.case: Paul does not rest his case on local taste alone. He cites the order of the Godhead in verse 3, the creation of man and woman in verses 7 to 9, the angels in verse 10, and the practice of all the churches in verse 16. Reasons so broad, on this reading, show that a visible sign of the order belongs to Christian worship wherever it is held.

views.label: A cultural form of a principle
views.case: The shame Paul describes depends on what a bare or covered head meant in Corinth, and he appeals to nature and propriety, which are cultural judgments. Where a covering no longer says what it said then, the principle of honoring the God-given distinction should be carried out in forms that do speak that way today.

views.label: The hair is the covering
views.case: Verse 15 says that long hair is given to the woman as a covering, peribolaion. Some therefore read the whole passage as being about hair worn up or cropped, and about the distinction of the sexes in appearance, and not about a separate veil.

debates.bearing: All three readings guard what Paul guards: the distinction of man and woman is honored in worship, and no one is humiliated. Congregations should hold their own custom without condemning the others, as verse 16 itself warns.

debates.question: What does head mean in verse 3?

views.label: Authority
views.case: The series runs from God through Christ and man to woman, and the surrounding language of honor, shame and glory suggests rank in a relationship. On this reading headship is real authority, modelled on the Father and the Son.

views.label: Source
views.case: Verse 8 says woman came from man and verse 12 says man is born of woman, which are statements about origin. Some read head here as source, in the sense of where something comes from, and point out that Christ is the source of every man, 1 Corinthians 8:6.

views.label: Prominence or representative
views.case: Others take head as the one who stands first or represents, the one by whom the group is known, so that the point is about honor and identity before it is about command.

debates.bearing: Whichever sense is preferred, Paul puts Christ and God in the series, so it cannot mean inferior worth. Interpreters who see authority still see it modelled on Christ's gift of himself, Ephesians 5:25.

debates.question: What does because of the angels mean in verse 10?

views.label: Guardians of order
views.case: Paul says elsewhere that the church is a spectacle to angels, 1 Corinthians 4:9, and that angels look into the gospel, 1 Peter 1:12. Holy angels are present at worship and watch that God's order is kept.

views.label: Fallen angels
views.case: Some early readers linked the angels to Genesis 6:1 to 4, as though unveiled women might tempt them. This view has little support in the text itself, which says nothing about temptation.

views.label: Messengers or witnesses
views.case: A few interpreters take the angels as human messengers or as heavenly observers who witness the church's honor before God.

debates.bearing: Paul gives the reason in a single phrase and does not explain it, so we should hold our conclusion lightly. The surest point is that worship is public before heaven as well as before neighbors.

study.originalLanguages:
The verbs of covering carry most of the passage. In verse 4 a man who prays or prophesies kata kephales echon, literally having something down from the head. The Greek does not name the object, and translators supply the idea of a covering. In verse 5 the woman is akatakalyptos, unveiled, from katakalyptein, to cover completely, the same verb that appears in the parallel statement of verse 6. The verse says a woman who will not be covered might as well have her hair cut, so the second half of the verse shows that Paul has an added covering in mind and not merely long hair. Yet in verse 15 he says that long hair is given to the woman as a covering, peribolaion, a wrap or mantle, the word used of a cloak in Hebrews 1:12. The word is used for something thrown around, and the question is whether he is saying hair replaces a veil or that hair gives nature's own pattern.

The word head works on two levels in verses 3 to 5. Kephale can mean the literal head, and in the series of verse 3 it stands for a person in relation to others. The play in verses 4 and 5 depends on the reader holding both senses together. Whether the figurative sense means authority, source or prominence is debated, and the verses that follow, verses 8 and 12, make source one real candidate, though in the series the Father is called the head of Christ, who was not made by Him.

In verse 10 the odd phrase is exousian echein epi tes kephales, a woman ought to have exousia on her head. The BSB footnote notes the alternative reading, or have authority over, since the Greek construction can be read more than one way. The word exousia is not elsewhere used for a veil as a symbol of someone else's authority, and a good many scholars take it as her own authority to pray and prophesy, shown by an act that suits the setting.

Verse 11 opens with plen, however, a small word that turns the whole argument. Paul does not take back what he has said; he sets a counterweight beside it. The word translated nature in verse 14 is phusis. Paul uses it elsewhere for what is naturally fitting and for what one is by birth, Galatians 2:15 and Romans 2:14, so here it means the instinctive sense of what is proper more than natural science.

Finally, verses 2 and 16 stand on the vocabulary of tradition. Paul commends them for keeping the paradoseis, the handed down things, and that noun comes from paradidomi, the verb he uses in 11:23 and 15:3 for passing on the gospel. Here, then, the church's practice in worship is treated as part of what is handed on.

typology.type: Man as the image and glory of God, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: Paul recalls Genesis 1:26 and 27, where humanity is made in the image of God. The pattern points to Christ, who is called the image of the invisible God, Colossians 1:15, and the one who shows God's glory in His face, 2 Corinthians 4:4 and 6. The escalation is that Adam bore the image as a creature, while the Son is that image by nature, and believers are being conformed to His likeness, Romans 8:29. The type falls short because the first man's image was marred at the fall, Genesis 3, and could not by itself reveal God to others.

typology.type: Woman from man and man through woman, verses 8 and 12
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 2:21 and 22 tells how the woman was built from the man's side, and Paul answers in verse 12 that man now comes through woman. Both strands meet in Christ, who was born of a woman, Galatians 4:4, the offspring promised in Genesis 3:15. The second Adam enters the world through the same channel as every man and so honors it. The type is not an exact fit, since Christ had no human father, so His birth fulfills the pattern by transcending it, Luke 1:35.

typology.type: The husband as head, the church as body, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Paul takes up the word head again in Ephesians 5:23 to 32, where the husband's headship is held up beside Christ's love for the church, for whom He gave Himself up. Genesis 2:24, quoted in Ephesians 5:31, is read as pointing beyond marriage to a mystery about Christ and the church. The escalation is that human headship at its best is only an image, and the original is Christ's self-giving. The type falls short because no husband is a saviour, and the picture of Christ and the church is not a command about power.

typology.type: The veil of Moses and the unveiled face, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Exodus 34:33 to 35 describes Moses wearing a veil when he spoke to the people after meeting God. In 2 Corinthians 3:12 to 18 Paul says that those in Christ, with unveiled faces, see and reflect the Lord's glory. The correspondence is loose, and the veils are not the same: Moses covered a fading glory, while the Corinthian covering concerns honor in the assembly. It is useful as a caution. The passage cannot be read as though to be veiled were to be shut out from God, since in Christ every believer has direct access to Him.

study.christ:
This passage tells us more about Christ than a first reading suggests, because Paul sets Him inside the order he teaches. The head of every man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God, verse 3. Everything about the doctrine of the Son depends on how that last clause is understood. The New Testament elsewhere says that the Son is equal with the Father, John 10:30, and that He did not count equality with God something to be grasped but took the form of a servant and obeyed, Philippians 2:6 to 8. The incarnate Son says that He does only what He sees His Father doing, John 5:19. So the head of Christ is God speaks of the relationship in which the Son, as the sent one, gladly honors the Father, and not of lesser deity. The church has long guarded this line: to be under a head in the order of relationship is not to be less in nature. That matters for the whole passage, because it shows that ordered relationships can be a matter of love and honor and not of worth.

The passage also shows the Son as the true image. Man is the image and glory of God, verse 7, and Paul elsewhere calls Christ the image of God in whom that likeness is complete, 2 Corinthians 4:4, Colossians 1:15. The first man shared the glory; the Son is the radiance of it, Hebrews 1:3.

Christ is also the one who made all things and by whom we exist, 1 Corinthians 8:6, and He was born of a woman, Galatians 4:4, so verse 12 meets its fulfillment in the incarnation. And He bore shame so that His people might not, Hebrews 12:2. The concern in this passage with who is honored and who is shamed finds its answer in the cross, where the Lord of glory took the place of dishonor. Finally, the order will be completed in Him: when all things are subjected, the Son Himself will be subject to the one who put everything under Him, so that God may be all in all, 1 Corinthians 15:28. We should not press the details of the veil into a picture of Christ, but the order, the image and the honor all point to Him.
study.god:
The passage presents God as the source of all order and honor. The final clause of verse 12, but everything comes from God, sets the limit for everything else Paul says. Whatever is said about headship, creation or custom, nothing is independent of Him, and no one in the assembly has a claim over another that is not derived. This is why verse 11 can say that in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman. God's design is relational, not solitary.

The passage also shows that God cares about how He is worshiped. He is not indifferent to the look and manner of gatherings; Paul will say in 14:33 that God is not a God of disorder, but of peace, and in 14:40 that everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner. This is not fussiness. God is honored when His people worship in ways that do not wound each other or confuse outsiders. Yet verse 16 reminds us that He is also not served by contention, and the Lord who gave the order does not want it enforced by quarrelling.

The passage reveals God's inner life as a pattern of honor. The Father is the head of Christ, and the Son is not made less by it, which means that God is not the kind of authority that diminishes those under it. This is a doctrine of the Trinity worth holding on to: the Father, Son and Spirit are one God, and the relations between them are marked by love and by glad giving of glory, John 17:4 and 5. A people made in His image are meant to reflect that, so men and women honor each other, and neither imagines that being under or over someone settles worth.

God made humanity male and female in His image, Genesis 1:27, and He hears and uses the prayer and prophecy of both. He is the God who cares about bodies, hair and heads, because He made them. It is a tension in the text, and we should not smooth it out, that God establishes order and yet binds each to the other in dependence. For worship this means gladness in the way He has made us, humility about our own place, and a readiness to give up our own preferences when they would make a brother or sister stumble.

crossReferences.note: The source of the image language in verse 7. God makes humanity in His image, male and female together, and gives both the work of ruling the creation. This is the baseline against which verse 7 must be read: whatever order Paul teaches, he cannot be denying that woman bears the same image.

The account behind verses 8 and 9. The woman is built from the man and brought to him, and is called bone of his bones. Paul takes the order of creation seriously, but verse 12 shows he holds it beside the fact that every man since has been born of a woman.

Paul's fullest teaching on headship in marriage. It begins with mutual submission and ends with Christ giving Himself up for the church, so the head here is the one who serves. It helps us read the word head in 1 Corinthians 11:3 without hearing only rank.

Paul declares that in Christ the old dividing lines of Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female no longer separate people. This verse tells us that the distinction Paul upholds in worship is not a distinction in standing before God. Both texts need to be held, one about equal access and worth, the other about how that unity is expressed in the assembly.

God promises to pour out His Spirit on sons and daughters, who will prophesy. Peter quotes it at Pentecost, Acts 2:17 and 18. It explains why Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy aloud in verse 5, and why his concern is how and not whether.

Philip the evangelist has four unmarried daughters who prophesied. It is a plain example from the same period of women speaking for God in the church, and it supports the reading that Paul is regulating their manner and not forbidding the practice.

A neighbouring passage that speaks of women being silent in the churches. Together with chapter 11 it forms a puzzle for interpreters, since chapter 11 assumes women prophesy. Some limit the silence to the testing of prophecy, others to disorderly questions, but any reading has to explain both.

The Son will hand the kingdom to the Father and be subject to Him so that God may be all in all. This is the fullest picture of verse 3, the head of Christ is God, and shows that submission within God is the glad completion of all things and not a lessening of the Son.

The Son, in the form of God, did not grasp at equality but took the form of a servant, and the Father highly exalted Him. It is the model for how an ordered relationship can carry honor and not diminish worth, which is the point Paul wants Corinth to see in verse 3.

Moses' veil is set against the unveiled faces of those in Christ, who see the Lord's glory and are transformed. It cautions against reading the covering as a barrier before God, and it shares with 1 Corinthians 11 a concern for glory in the presence of the Lord.

Another passage that mentions women's dress in worship and appeals to the creation order, 1 Timothy 2:13. It shows that Paul's creation argument is not confined to Corinth, though the passage has its own difficulties and its own setting in Ephesus.

God sent His Son, born of a woman. It fulfills verse 12, man is born of woman, in the most remarkable way: the One who is the head of every man enters the world as a child of a woman, and so honors the order of creation as well as its origin.

study.oneStory:
The passage touches nearly every part of the biblical story. At creation, God made humanity in His image, male and female, Genesis 1:27, and set man and woman side by side with a different origin and a shared calling. Paul quotes this to show that distinction was in the plan from the start, and that it is good. At the fall the question of shame enters the world: the first thing the pair did after eating was to see that they were naked and to cover themselves, Genesis 3:7. When Paul speaks here of shame, of covering and of honor, he is writing in a world that still lives in the aftermath of that scene, and the passage can be read as an effort to help the church worship in ways that do not add to that old shame.

Redemption changes the picture in two ways that Paul wants held together. The Spirit is poured out on sons and daughters, Acts 2:17, so women now pray and prophesy before the whole assembly, and the church is one body in which Jews and Greeks, slave and free, male and female stand equally before God, Galatians 3:28. Yet redemption does not dissolve creation; the God who redeems is the God who made us male and female, and so the church keeps a glad difference within a deeper unity. The head of every man is Christ, who humbled Himself and was exalted, Philippians 2:8 and 9, and under whose headship the whole order of the church is healed.

Looking ahead, the passage points toward a time when every veil is gone. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 3:18 that we are already seeing the Lord's glory with unveiled faces, and in 1 Corinthians 13:12 that we shall see face to face. In the new creation God's servants will see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the elders cast their crowns before the throne, Revelation 4:10, because all glory belongs to Him. The order of verse 3 reaches its end when the Son hands the kingdom to the Father so that God may be all in all, 1 Corinthians 15:28. Until then, worship is a rehearsal in which men and women learn to give honor, and to receive it, under one Lord.

quiz.q: What order of headship does Paul set out in verse 3?

options.text: God is the head of Christ, Christ of man, and man of woman.
options.note: Paul names an ordered series from God to Christ to man to woman.

options.text: Christ is the head of man, and man the head of woman.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the crowning link, that the head of Christ is God.

options.text: There is no order; all relationships are identical.
options.note: Paul does teach an order, while also affirming interdependence.

options.text: Man is the head of God, Christ, and woman.
options.note: This reverses the order; God is the head of Christ.

quiz.q: How does the phrase the head of Christ is God guard against misreading headship?

options.text: It shows headship need not mean lesser worth, since the Son is fully God yet honors the Father.
options.note: Christ's equal deity within the order rules out any idea of inferiority.

options.text: It models headship as a relationship of honor rather than domination.
options.note: A true implication, resting on the deeper point that the Son is fully equal in deity.

options.text: It has nothing to do with how we understand headship.
options.note: It is precisely the pattern that shapes a right reading of headship.

options.text: It proves Christ is inferior to the Father in His being.
options.note: Orthodox faith confesses the Son as fully equal in deity.

quiz.q: How does Paul balance the order of headship in verses 11 and 12?

options.text: In the Lord man and woman are interdependent, and everything comes from God.
options.note: Woman came from man, man is born of woman, all from God.

options.text: By stressing that man too is born of woman, so neither can boast.
options.note: True to verse 12, though the full balance adds that everything comes from God.

options.text: By saying women are independent of men entirely.
options.note: He says neither is independent of the other.

options.text: By declaring the order of headship abolished.
options.note: He balances the order with interdependence, not abolishes it.

quiz.q: Which is a fair way to handle the head covering itself for today?

options.text: Hold firmly to the principle of honoring God's order and distinction, while recognizing Christians differ on the covering's binding form.
options.note: The abiding principle is clear; the form is where the church debates fairly.

options.text: Continue the covering itself, since Paul grounds it in creation and the angels.
options.note: A respectable orthodox reading; others hold the veil was the cultural expression of the abiding principle.

options.text: Insist everyone must agree the veil is merely cultural.
options.note: Orthodox readers differ; humility here is fitting.

options.text: Treat head coverings as the heart of the gospel.
options.note: The custom is not the gospel; the principle serves honorable worship.

quiz.q: According to the passage, do women take an active part in public worship?

options.text: Yes; women pray and prophesy in the assembly, and the question is how, not whether.
options.note: Verse 5 assumes women praying and prophesying; Paul addresses the manner.

options.text: Yes, though the manner is to be weighed with Paul's other instructions on order.
options.note: Rightly affirms their participation; this passage regulates the how, to be read alongside his wider teaching.

options.text: No; women are entirely silent here.
options.note: This passage assumes women praying and prophesying.

options.text: Only men may pray or prophesy.
options.note: Verse 5 speaks of women who pray or prophesy.

questions: Paul commends the Corinthians for holding the traditions he handed on. What faithful teaching have you received that you are called to keep and pass on?
The head of Christ is God, yet the Son is fully equal with the Father. How does Christ's glad honoring of the Father reshape the way you think about order and honor among God's people?
In the Lord man and woman are not independent of one another, and everything comes from God. Where might pride or rivalry between the sexes need to give way to glad interdependence?
This passage wraps a lasting principle in a cultural custom. How can you hold firmly to what honors God while showing humility toward fellow Christians who apply the details differently?
Worship is meant to render honor rightly to God and one another. What in your own worship, in attitude or action, might God be calling you to bring into greater honor and order?

translationNotes.note: Head translates kephale, used relationally in an ordered series; interpreters weigh whether it stresses authority or source, but the pattern is one of honor, safeguarded from any idea of unequal worth by the head of Christ being God.

The verse assumes women praying and prophesying in the gathering; Paul is regulating the manner of their participation, not forbidding it, which must be weighed alongside his instructions elsewhere on order in worship.

A sign of authority on her head can be read either as the authority she stands under or as her own authority to pray and prophesy; the reference to the angels likely concerns due order and reverence in worship.
